description: What logo design costs in 2026, from AI tools to agencies, what each budget gets you, what branding costs beyond the logo, and how to compare quotes.
body:
Logo design cost depends on the scope you buy, not on the logo itself.

A tool download, a custom mark and a complete identity with colors, typography and guidelines are three different purchases.

So compare the deliverables first, then compare the fees.

This guide gives you market planning ranges for each level, what each level actually includes, and the questions that expose a weak quote.

I'm Arek Dvornechuck, founder and creative director of Ebaqdesign, a branding and Webflow studio in Brooklyn, and I've been designing logos and identities for about 20 years.

If you're comparing local specialists, see my roundup of brand identity designers in NYC.

How much does logo design cost in 2026?

Here's what the market charges at each level, in USD, as planning guidance rather than a quote.

ProviderTypical market rangeWhat you usually get
AI tools$0 to $100Self-directed design; downloads and licenses vary.
Entry-level freelancer$100 to $1,000A narrow brief, limited exploration and a basic handoff.
Senior designer$1,000 to $5,000Custom exploration, refinement, variations and final files.
Expert or studio$5,000 to $25,000Deeper discovery and direction; confirm the identity deliverables.
Branding firm$25,000+Strategy, identity system, guidelines and key applications.
Top-tier agency$100,000+Complex strategy, identity programs, stakeholder alignment and rollout.

These are approximate market bands, not surveyed averages and not my studio's pricing.

They overlap because experience, location, complexity and deliverables vary.

Large rebrands can go far beyond these figures.

For a low-end reference, Looka's published help page lists a $20 basic PNG package and a $65 premium package with more files and variations.

That's a product purchase, not a designer engagement, so check current checkout pricing and inclusions before you buy.

Logo only or full brand identity?

A logo is one part of a brand identity, so two proposals with "branding" on the cover can solve very different problems.

A logo-only project can include a primary mark, alternate lockups, a small-size version, color variations and a practical file package.

A brand identity system adds the rules that make the business recognizable beyond the mark: typography, color, imagery, layout and applications.

Discovery workshops, positioning, naming, messaging, packaging, website design, motion and rollout support are extra scope unless the proposal says otherwise.

If your positioning is already clear and your visual guidelines already work, a focused logo project may be enough.

If every deck, social post and web page looks like a different company, a new mark alone won't fix it.

For the wider deliverables, see my guide to what a branding package includes.

What do you get at each budget?

Pick the level of help your business needs, including how much of the brief and the decisions you can handle yourself.

Under $1,000: AI tools or entry-level help

AI tools, templates, entry-level freelancers and contest packages can suit an early experiment or a tightly defined small project.

The upside is a smaller upfront spend and, sometimes, a fast result.

The tradeoffs are less exploration, little real guidance, thin file packages and imagery other businesses may also be using.

Before you buy, check whether you can use the elements commercially, whether they're exclusive, and whether the files work in print as well as on screen.

A low price doesn't automatically mean bad work, but it makes a clear, limited scope essential.

$1,000 to $5,000: a focused project with a senior designer

This is a practical range to explore when you want a senior designer to build a distinctive mark around a defined brief.

When choosing a logo designer, look for relevant work, a clear explanation of design decisions, an agreed refinement process and examples of finished handoffs.

You get direct collaboration and more chances to test the design against your audience, your competitors and your real uses.

You'll still need to give thoughtful feedback, and a full identity or website usually sits outside the quote.

$5,000 and up: studio support and broader scope

An expert or studio brings deeper exploration, strategic guidance, stakeholder alignment and more demanding production experience.

At this level, ask exactly how much of the fee covers the logo and how much covers strategy, identity development, applications or rollout.

The extra investment makes sense when you have a consequential launch, recognition to protect, or several teams who need to use the identity the same way.

More people and more deliverables also mean more coordination, so a big agency process can be overkill for a simple, well-defined need.

How much does branding cost beyond the logo?

For most companies, the logo is the smallest line in the real branding budget.

The mark has to show up on a website, a pitch deck, social, product screens, ads and sales material, and every one of those is design work.

Here's what usually sits around the logo in a full brand launch:

  • Brand strategy: positioning, audience, messaging and the story you tell investors and customers.
  • Identity system: typography, color, imagery, layout rules and guidelines your team can actually follow.
  • Website: design and build, which for most startups is the single biggest piece of brand spend.
  • Motion: animated logo, product videos and social content that make the brand feel alive.
  • Rollout: decks, templates, signage, packaging and whatever else carries the brand into the world.

Budget for the whole launch, not just the mark.

The most expensive branding is the kind you pay for twice: a cheap logo first, then a full rebuild when it can't stretch across the rest of the business.

Why investing in logo design matters

Your logo gives people a consistent visual cue everywhere they meet your business.

It helps customers recognize you, ties your communications together and separates your offer from nearby competitors.

Like a good storefront, it sets expectations before anyone has tried the product.

But it has to work on a tiny profile image, a proposal, packaging, signage and anything else you actually use.

Recognition comes from a useful mark applied consistently, backed by the experience your business delivers.

A logo can't repair a weak offer on its own, which is why I start with the business problem, not a favorite symbol.

What changes the price of a logo?

The fee reflects the decisions and work needed to reach a usable result, not the number of lines in the final mark.

Experience and responsibility

An experienced designer knows what to explore, what to throw out and how to defend the final direction.

Ask who will actually do the work and present it, especially when comparing a freelancer with an agency team.

Research and strategic clarity

Competitor reviews, audience interviews, market context and positioning work take time, but they define what the design needs to say.

If you already have solid strategy, share it so the designer builds on it instead of repeating discovery.

Concepts, revisions and approvals

Define how many directions you'll see, how feedback is collected and what counts as one revision round.

For example, a proposal might include two directions and two rounds of refinement on the one you pick, with anything beyond that scoped separately.

A new direction after approval is not a refinement, so agree up front on how brief changes are handled.

Applications, rights and deadlines

A logo tested for embroidery, packaging, multiple languages and a mobile app is a different job from a single website wordmark.

Get ownership and licensing terms in writing, including any third-party typefaces or assets.

Rush delivery, several decision-makers and a fixed launch date all change the workload and the price.

What should your logo package include?

Agree on the handoff before work starts, so you don't discover a missing format when a printer or developer asks for it.

  • Final logo variations: the approved primary mark, alternate lockups and any agreed icon or small-size version.
  • Scalable vector artwork: SVG and a print-ready vector format, plus editable source files if contracted.
  • Raster exports: transparent PNG files and the other sizes your team actually needs.
  • Color versions: full color, black and reversed white versions that stay legible on your backgrounds.
  • Basic usage guidance: clear space, minimum size, color values and examples of incorrect use.
  • Written terms: the approved artwork covered by the agreement, rights granted, payment milestones and third-party licenses.

Vector files scale without pixelation, but having a vector file doesn't mean your trademark is cleared.

A full identity manual, social templates, a custom typeface or a website should each appear as its own deliverable when you need them.

Why a simple logo can take substantial work

The final mark looks effortless because the designer removed every idea and detail that didn't help.

The logo design process moves from understanding the business to exploring concepts, refining one direction and testing the artwork in use.

Sketching, type studies, proportion tweaks, color decisions and vector construction all feed the result.

Technical checks matter too, because a mark that looks great on a big slide can fall apart in a browser tab or in one-color print.

Ask how the designer tests against those constraints, rather than judging value by the number of concepts.

Pay for a sound process and a useful outcome, not for the promise that a pricier logo guarantees a more successful business.

How to budget for your logo project

Start with the business need and work outward to the full cost of getting the design into use.

1. Write a short brief

Explain what you sell, who you need to reach, how you're different, what the logo should communicate and why you're doing it now.

List the real uses, such as a website header, social avatar, storefront, packaging or deck template.

2. Separate launch essentials from later additions

Decide what must be ready for launch and what can wait, including secondary applications and future brand extensions.

Leave room for implementation, production, licenses and any specialist work you'll commission separately.

3. Agree on a realistic schedule

Ask for a project calendar covering discovery, concept presentation, feedback, refinement and final delivery.

A focused logo project can move in a few weeks, while a broader identity with several approval layers can take months.

Use the designer's schedule for your scope instead of assuming a universal turnaround, and check what happens if your feedback runs late.

4. Compare total scope, not just the first fee

For a fixed-fee project, confirm what triggers extra charges and when payments are due.

For hourly work, ask for an estimated range and an approval point before it's exceeded.

Factor in what it costs to replace signage, packaging and other materials later, not only the design fee.

Questions to ask before accepting a quote

Send the same brief to a short list, so every proposal answers the same buying decision.

Ask these questions when you compare proposals:

  • Is this a logo-only project or a broader identity engagement?
  • Who designs the work, and which relevant projects can I review?
  • What research, concepts, revisions and meetings are included?
  • Which final files, variations and usage guidelines will I receive?
  • What rights and third-party licenses are included?
  • What is excluded, and how is extra work approved and priced?
  • What happens after launch, and can the same team keep supporting the brand?
  • What are the milestones, feedback deadlines and payment terms?

A specific answer beats "unlimited revisions" or a long list of file extensions without a clear scope.

If you're a designer working out your own fees, my logo pricing guide covers that side of the conversation.

What famous logo prices actually tell you

Historic logo prices are fun trivia, but they're a poor substitute for a quote built around your business.

Nike's own archive confirms that Carolyn Davidson invoiced $35 for the original Swoosh in 1971.

That figure describes one commission in one year, not the cost of building Nike's recognition over decades.

NeXT's $100,000 commission brought Paul Rand's identity expertise to Steve Jobs's new company, as documented by the People's Graphic Design Archive.

London 2012's roughly £400,000 covered a broader identity: Parliament's 2007 answer gives the design cost, and the London Assembly's scope explanation includes the Olympic and Paralympic emblems and core brand identity.

Pepsi reportedly paid $1 million for its 2008 redesign.

BP reportedly spent $7 million on its 2000 brand change.

These are historical amounts in original currencies, not adjusted for inflation, and their scopes are too different to rank side by side.

Widely repeated corporate "logo costs" often include naming, strategy, brand systems or rollout, so don't compare them with a standalone design fee.

Your budget should follow your brief, not the cheapest or most spectacular number on a famous-logo list.

Logo design cost FAQ

Is a cheap logo good enough for a startup?

It can be for a quick test, but once you're raising money or selling high-ticket services, a generic mark costs you credibility in every pitch and sales call.

How long does a professional logo take?

A focused logo or identity project can move in a few weeks when the brief is clear and decisions are quick, while bigger identity programs with many stakeholders take longer.

Why don't you list your prices?

Because scope drives the number, and a fixed quote after a short call is more honest than a list that fits nobody exactly.

Should I hire a freelancer or a studio?

A freelancer can be great for a contained logo, while a studio makes more sense when you need the logo, website and motion to work as one system over time.
